nameStory: The southern blue flag gets its "flag" name from its large, banner-like petals that flutter in wetland breezes like colorful flags. "Southern" distinguishes it from its close cousin, the northern blue flag, though both species actually overlap quite a bit in New England's marshes and pond edges.
description: Southern blue flag is a stunning wetland perennial that produces spectacular blue-violet flowers in late spring and early summer. Growing 2-4 feet tall, it forms clumps of sword-like leaves that emerge directly from the ground. The flowers are the real showstoppers - large, intricate blooms with three drooping petals and three upright petals, all decorated with delicate veining. Like all irises, it grows from thick underground stems called rhizomes.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large blue-violet flowers with six petals in two layers - three drooping 'falls' and three upright 'standards'. The falls often have intricate purple veining and may have white or yellow patches near the center. Flowers are 3-4 inches across and have a sweet, light fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, sword-shaped leaves that are flat and smooth to the touch, growing directly from the base in a fan pattern. Leaves are blue-green in color and have prominent parallel veins running their length. They feel firm and somewhat waxy.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense clumps 2-4 feet tall in wetland areas. Multiple flowering stems emerge from each clump, with each stem typically bearing 2-3 flowers that open in succession.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces three-chambered capsules that split open to reveal brown, disc-shaped seeds. The capsules are initially green and plump, turning brown and papery as they mature in late summer.

habitat: Southern blue flag thrives in New England's wetlands, particularly along pond edges, in marshes, wet meadows, and shallow swampy areas. It prefers full sun to partial shade and rich, consistently moist to wet soils. You'll often find it growing alongside cattails, pickerelweed, and various sedges in these soggy spots.

seasonality.spring: New sword-like leaves emerge from the wet soil, growing rapidly as the weather warms. Flower buds begin forming on tall stems in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in early summer with spectacular blue-violet flowers lasting several weeks. After flowering, green seed capsules develop while leaves remain lush and green.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules turn brown and split open to release seeds. Leaves begin to yellow and die back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only the underground rhizomes to survive the cold. Look for brown, dried seed stalks poking through snow.

funFact: This iris was one of just three flower species used in Ronald Fisher's famous 1936 statistical study that helped create modern data science - your smartphone's facial recognition technology traces back to mathematical techniques first tested on southern blue flag petals!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with northern blue flag, but southern blue flag typically has broader petals and the falls (drooping petals) are usually wider than they are long. Northern blue flag falls tend to be longer than wide. When in doubt, check if you can fit your thumb width across a drooping petal - if yes, it's likely southern blue flag.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "southern" blue flag, this species actually grows well into northern New England and overlaps extensively with "northern" blue flag. The names refer more to their overall continental ranges than where you'll find them locally - both can grow in the same wetland!
compareHints: Compared to northern blue flag, southern blue flag typically has broader, more rounded flower petals and slightly wider leaves. Yellow iris is much taller with bright yellow flowers and can form massive colonies. The various cultivated garden irises (like Siberian iris) usually prefer drier soils and have different bloom times or colors.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Northern blue flag is much larger and more robust than slender blue flag, which has narrow, grass-like leaves and smaller flowers.
Yellow iris is the only consistently yellow-flowered iris you'll find growing wild in New England wetlands - all our native iris species like northern blue flag have blue or purple flowers.
Japanese Iris differs from Northern Blue Flag by its gray-green (rather than bright green) leaves and reddish-purple flower tones instead of pure blue-purple.
Slender blue flag is much more delicate than the common northern blue flag, with leaves that are dramatically narrower (pencil-width vs.

Unlike its freshwater-loving cousins like northern blue flag (which grows in marshes and pond edges), beach-head iris is the only New England iris that can survive in pure beach sand with constant salt exposure.
Dwarf crested iris is dramatically smaller than all other New England irises - while northern blue flag and yellow iris tower at 2-4 feet tall in wetlands, this woodland species stays under 6 inches.
Unlike New England's native blue flag irises which are tall wetland plants, netted iris is tiny and prefers dry, well-drained soils.
Unlike other New England irises that have blue, purple, or yellow flowers, blackberry lily is the only one with orange, spotted blooms.
Sweet iris differs from New England's native blue flag irises by its sweet fragrance and slightly more purple-tinted flowers.
Siberian iris differs from Northern Blue Flag by having much narrower, more grass-like leaves and more compact growth, while Yellow Iris has broader leaves and bright yellow flowers.
Japanese iris differs from native blue flags by its massive, completely flat flowers and preference for consistently wet, acidic soil.
Unlike our common northern blue flag with its blue-purple flowers or the invasive yellow iris with bright yellow blooms, cemetery iris stands out with pure white flowers.
